reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A restrictive cardiomyopathy characterised by dense fibrosis of the ventricular endocardium, particularly at the apices and inflow tracts
One of the most common causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy worldwide, seen predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions
Both ventricles may be affected; right-sided disease produces prominent systemic venous congestion and ascites, while left-sided disease causes pulmonary congestion
Fibrosis obliterating the apex and tethering the atrioventricular valves leads to restrictive filling and mitral or tricuspid regurgitation
Atrial dilatation is often striking, and atrial fibrillation and mural thrombus with embolism are common complications
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI reveal apical obliteration, endocardial thickening, and restrictive physiology
It is regarded as related to eosinophilic endomyocardial disease, representing a chronic fibrotic end stage of endocardial injury
Surgical resection of fibrous tissue with valve repair or replacement may help selected patients with advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Endomyocardial fibrosis involves progressive deposition of fibrous tissue in the endocardium and subendocardial myocardium of one or both ventricular apices and inflow regions. The condition is linked to eosinophilic endomyocardial injury, and factors such as infection, dietary, and environmental influences have been proposed in endemic areas. The rigid fibrotic endocardium restricts diastolic filling, obliterates the ventricular apex, and distorts the subvalvular apparatus, causing atrioventricular regurgitation. Impaired filling raises atrial pressures, producing marked atrial enlargement, congestion, and a predisposition to arrhythmia and thrombus.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac amyloidosis and other infiltrative restrictive cardiomyopathies
Right heart failure from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography for apical obliteration, endocardial thickening, and restrictive filling
Cardiac MRI to define fibrosis and differentiate from other restrictive disease
ECG and monitoring for atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias
Full blood count to detect eosinophilia
Evaluation for mural thrombus and embolic risk
redFlags: Progressive restrictive heart failure with refractory congestion or ascites
reference.prognosis: Advanced endomyocardial fibrosis carries a guarded prognosis, particularly with severe valvular involvement and biventricular disease. Medical therapy is largely supportive for heart failure and complications, and while surgery can relieve symptoms in selected patients, operative risk is significant and the fibrotic process may recur.
pitfalls: Mistaking the restrictive picture for constrictive pericarditis, which is surgically curable
Overlooking mural thrombus and embolic risk
Failing to recognise the link with eosinophilic disease in earlier stages
Underestimating the contribution of valvular regurgitation to symptoms
Delaying evaluation in patients from endemic regions with unexplained right heart failure
